blocks.tk: Türkmenler nakyllary gowy görýärler. Nakyla “atalar sözi” hem diýilýär. Gürrüňde bir ýagdaý barada pikiriňi gysga we owadan aýtmak üçin nakyl getirýärler. Nakyl köplenç “… diýen nakyl bar” ýa-da “… diýilýär” diýlip getirilýär. Onuň manysy köplenç şol ýagdaýdan düşnükli bolýar. Aşakda on iki meşhur nakyl we olaryň manysy bar.
blocks.en: Turkmen call a proverb a nakyl, and also atalar sözi, the words of the ancestors; folklorists have long debated whether the two terms mean different things, and Didar Annaberdiyev's 2013 survey argues they are best treated as the same. In conversation a proverb sums up a situation in a few well-chosen words, and, as the folklorist Kakaly Berkeliýew noted, its meaning often becomes clear only from the situation it is used in. In writing, a proverb is often introduced as “…” diýen nakyl, the proverb that says “…”, or followed by diýilýär, it is said. Here are twelve well-known ones.
Who has not worked will not eat.
blocks.source: Traditional proverb; wording as in the Turkmen Wikipedia's collection “Nakyl”, also in L. Doğan's collection; our translation
Traditional proverb; wording as in the explanatory dictionary on enedilim.com (under ölçemek), also in L. Doğan's collection and, as “Ýedi ölçe-de, bir kes”, in the Turkmen Wikipedia; our translation

blocks.en: Apple, ripen and fall into my mouth.
blocks.source: Traditional proverb; wording as in the Turkmen Wikipedia's collection “Nakyl”, also in L. Doğan's collection; our translation

blocks.tk: Bu nakyllar zähmet we sabyr barada. Işlemän baý bolmak isleýän adama “Işlemedik – dişlemez” diýýärler. “Ýedi ölçäp, bir kes” diýip, möhüm karar bermezden öň oýlanmagy maslahat berýärler. “Alma biş, agzyma düş” bolsa hiç zat etmän garaşyp oturan adam barada aýdylýar.
blocks.en: These three are about work and patience. The first, literally “who has not worked will not bite”, is what people say to someone who wants the rewards without the effort. The second is advice to think twice before an important decision. The third mocks someone who sits and waits for good things to come by themselves.

blocks.tk: Akylla bir söz bes, akmaga müň söz hebes.
blocks.en: For the wise, one word is enough; for a fool, a thousand are wasted.
blocks.source: Traditional proverb, marked as a nakyl in the explanatory dictionary on enedilim.com (under hebes); also in L. Doğan's collection and, as “… besdir, … hebesdir”, in the Turkmen Wikipedia; our translation
Traditional proverb; wording as in the Turkmen Wikipedia's collection “Nakyl”; also in L. Doğan's collection, with diýen; our translation

blocks.tk: Dagy-daşy ýel bozar, adam arasyny – söz.
blocks.en: Wind wears down mountains and stones; words wear down what lies between people.
blocks.source: Traditional proverb; wording as in the Turkmen Wikipedia's collection “Nakyl”, also in L. Doğan's collection; our translation

blocks.tk: Bu üç nakyl söz barada. Akylly adama köp düşündirmek gerek däl, akmak bolsa müň sözden hem düşünmez. Diňe gürlemek ýeterlik däl, işi hem etmeli. Ýaman söz bolsa adamlaryň arasyny bozýar.
blocks.en: These three are about words. The first says a wise person understands from a single word, while a fool won't understand a thousand; hebes is an old word for pointless. The second reminds you that talking about something is not doing it. The third warns that gossip and harsh words damage friendships, the way wind wears down stone.
Tell a friend his faults to his face.
blocks.source: Traditional proverb; wording as in the Turkmen Wikipedia's collection “Nakyl”, also in L. Doğan's collection; our translation

blocks.en: Know a young man by his friend.
blocks.source: Traditional proverb; wording as in the Turkmen Wikipedia's collection “Nakyl”, also in L. Doğan's collection; our translation

blocks.en: A robe cut after taking advice is never too short.
blocks.source: Traditional proverb; wording as in the Turkmen Wikipedia's collection “Nakyl”, also in L. Doğan's collection; our translation

blocks.tk: El eli ýuwar, iki el birigip – ýüzi.
blocks.en: One hand washes the other, and two hands together wash the face.
blocks.source: Traditional proverb; wording as in the Turkmen Wikipedia's collection “Nakyl”, also in L. Doğan's collection; our translation

blocks.tk: Bu dört nakyl dostluk we maslahat barada. Hakyky dost seniň kemçiligiňi arkaňdan däl, ýüzüňe aýdar. Adamyň nähili adamdygyny onuň dostlaryndan bilip bolýar. Möhüm işe başlamazdan öň maslahatlaşmak gerek. Adamlar biri-birine kömek etseler, has köp iş edip bilerler.
blocks.en: These four are about friends and advice. A true friend tells you your faults to your face, not behind your back. You can tell what a person is like from the friends they keep. Before starting something important, talk it over: a robe cut after taking advice comes out the right length. And people who help each other, like two hands washing a face, get more done.

blocks.tk: Süýtde agzy bişen, suwy üfläp içer.
blocks.en: Who has burned his mouth on milk blows on water before drinking it.
blocks.source: Traditional proverb; wording as in the Turkmen Wikipedia's collection “Nakyl”, also in L. Doğan's collection; our translation

blocks.en: The dog barks, the caravan moves on.
blocks.source: Traditional proverb; wording as in the Turkmen Wikipedia's collection “Nakyl”, also in L. Doğan's collection; our translation

blocks.tk: Iň soňky iki nakyl seresaplylyk we sabyr barada. Bir gezek ýalňyşan adam soňra has seresaply bolýar. Başgalaryň boş gürrüňine üns berme, öz işiňi dowam et.
blocks.en: The last two are about caution and calm. Someone who has been hurt once takes care even where there is no danger, like a person blowing on cold water. And if people talk behind your back, carry on with your work: the dog barks, but the caravan moves on.

blocks.title: Reading the Turkmen
blocks.text: Look for this unit's grammar: *diýilýär* and *diýlip* (it is said, said as), *diýip* before *maslahat berýärler*, and *adamyň nähili adamdygyny* (what kind of person someone is), a fact clause with `-dYgY`. Many proverbs drop a verb that is easy to guess: *iki el birigip – ýüzi*, two hands together (wash) the face.

vocab.en: proverb (literally the words of the ancestors)
to consult each other, to talk (something) over

questions.q: A friend is about to make a big decision in a hurry. Which proverb fits?
questions.explain: *Möhüm karar bermezden öň oýlanmagy maslahat berýärler*: measure seven times, cut once.

questions.q: What does *Bal diýmek bilen agyz süýjemez* say?
options: Talking about something isn't doing it.
questions.explain: *Diňe gürlemek ýeterlik däl, işi hem etmeli.*

questions.q: Which proverb is about helping each other?
options: El eli ýuwar, iki el birigip – ýüzi.
questions.explain: *Adamlar biri-birine kömek etseler, has köp iş edip bilerler.*
